corpus: Text2Vis.csv (mizanurr/Text2Vis, 1,985 rows, 1,470 scored after unmapped labels)
note: Raised by hand, in the commit that earns it. 529 was the reading after the corpus's Question column replaced its Prompt column: every rule reading in this repository had been taken on the whole conversational turn, table inlined, so a cue matched the table's own headers (a column called `Projected share of the population` fired `share`, which names a pie). The product reads 530 (36.05%) on the question; the cue table reads 575 (39.12%), so the gap is 3.07pp. The +1 is the round that taught `profileRows` to take the table's column order: a column every cell of which is null is no longer admitted as an axis or a measure, which moved one row. The denominator is compared for identity, not for a floor: a reading over a different row set is a different question. This reading is the round that stopped reading a pair of values as a scale: 145 tables of the corpus were two rows wide and had no measure at all, so every mark refused them. Reading a pair by what its numbers look like moved declined 167 -> 39 and, with it, top-1 530 -> 579 (+3.34pp) and shortlist 623 -> 676: a table that is refused cannot hit a family, so a fix to a refusal is also a fix to the counter. The render reading moves 1,286 -> 1,414 figures for the same reason, and the judge readings taken at 1,286 are kept as history rather than compared with the ones after it. 588/686/35 (v9.29): the melt's own reading, taken by the text2vis-rule job of run 44149995497 on 27defec5 and raised here because the number did not exist until that job ran. The melt re-marked 111 tables, not the 44 the census had counted: bar 698 -> 645, line 341 -> 452, pie 250 -> 227, scatter 66 -> 64, boxplot 43 -> 14, declined 39 -> 35. The census was counting tables that no admission rule could chart; the melt predicate is about the *column names* being periods, and 107 of those tables were being charted as the wrong mark rather than refused — a wide table with five or more columns fits a boxplot's tuple shape, which reads five years as min/q1/median/q3/max, and 29 rows were drawn that way. The reading is a net gain on the only labeled metric (top-1 579 -> 588, +0.61pp; shortlist 676 -> 686) and the four new figures are the ones that were declined. Floors raised here rather than in 27defec5 because a floor is a number taken from a reading, and this reading is the first one that exists. **v9.31: 588 -> 606, shortlist 686 -> 710, declined 35 -> 35.** Two typing rules in one change, because each one alone is a wash and together they are not. A column of years with *holes* in it — a survey fielded every two years, `2002, 2004, 2006, 2008, 2010` — is a timeline, and the rule demanded a contiguous block: ten rows gained against three lost when the gap clause is dropped. A *scale* steps by one, and the rule asked only whether the column repeated inside a small range, so a survey's percentages per wave (`10, 12, 9, 14` over eight rows, four distinct) were read as an axis and the measure they carried disappeared: that is what answered a two-measure scatter `heatmap` and a heatmap a `scatter`. Alone that reads 588 again (the losses are the gapped years the first rule recovers), together they read **606** on 27 gains against 9 losses — a paired comparison on the same rows, sign test p = 0.004. Family by family: line 58.82% -> 63.17%, scatter 23.66% -> 27.96%, bar 57.42% -> 55.46% (seven rows of year-by-several-measures now read a line where the corpus says a bar, which is label noise in both directions and the next round's job). Also fixed in this reading: the `delta by family` line compared the cue report's *covering* hit with this report's *strict* one and published the difference between the predicates as a difference between the instruments — it read `area -58`, which says the result set made the area family worse, and it did not. **v9.46: 606 -> 610, shortlist 710 -> 713, declined 35 -> 35.** The derived boxplot, and the row counts are the smallest part of it: the *Boxplot* family reads 6.74% -> 47.19% (+36 of its 89 rows) because a table that states its distribution by repeating a measure is now read as one, while the marks the old admission overruled pay for it — bar 198 -> 176, line 247 -> 243, stacked bar 36 -> 34, and 17 histogram rows that used to answer `gauge` now answer `boxplot`. Net +4 on top-1, and the swap is the cue table's own reading, not this change's: `distribution` names a boxplot, the admission refused every boxplot, and the cue was being overruled by a rule about columns. The ablation prices that cue at +25 rows (`no-distribution` reads 550), so the 28 rows it costs are the price of the 36 it wins. Shipped, the same change removes 144 of the 223 `not-admitted` vetoes, which is the half of this reading a rule arm cannot show. **v9.50 (round 179): the parser reads `nan` as a printed absence** — 595 cells in 320 columns of 120 rows — and a column whose every cell is an absence is not a column: 610 -> 614 top-1, 713 -> 718 shortlist, 35 -> 28 declined, shipped 807 unchanged, 13 rows drew a different chart (3 gained, 3 lost, 7 uncorked). The same round made `limit` count columns on a matrix and rows elsewhere. **v9.52: 614 -> 664, 718 -> 744, declined 28 -> 27.** The histogram reading. A question that names a histogram is now answered with one: every finite number in the table is pooled, counted into equal-width bins, and the bars are drawn over the bins (`histogramReading` in the chart package) instead of over the table's own columns. Nothing about the mark changed — a histogram is a bar with the measure binned, which is what the reference code does — and that is why the reading had to change with it: `familiesOfMark('bar', 'histogram')` now lists `histogram` first, because the picture *is* a histogram and a family list that led with `bar` was pricing the shortlist while the chart drew a grouped bar of the period columns. 50 of the corpus's 90 histogram rows are answered this way — exactly the rows whose question names the word — and 50 is the whole of the +50: no family lost a row, `declined` fell by one because a table of numbers with no admissible mark still has a distribution, and `shortlist` rose by 26 because a bar on a histogram question now claims the family rather than only covering it. The 40 rows that are still misses are rows where the cue did not fire (40 of 90 name the distribution some other way), not rows this reading failed on.

judge.note: The sixth full reading, run 44150185171 on 27defec5 with glm-4.5v, and the first taken after the melt: 1,418 figures rendered, 1,416 judged, 1,418 calls, two rows the provider's content policy would not look at (rows 1006 and 1007, refused at the prompt with `400 系统检测到输入或生成内容可能包含不安全或敏感内容` — a fact about the question, not about the figure, and counted rather than scored). chart_correctness 3.05 -> 3.44 and readability 6.05 -> 6.49, so the floor moves to 3.44/6.49: both dimensions rose on a population that is the same 1,418 rows the render floor names. **The +0.39 is not read off two means.** The two denominators differ by four figures and 140 rows changed mark, so the reading was taken as a paired difference over the 1,411 rows both readings graded (`pnpm bench:text2vis:ablate --before <fifth> --after <sixth>`): the 140 rows the melt re-drew moved correctness 1.78 -> 5.91 (+4.13 ± 0.93) and readability 4.61 -> 9.19 (+4.59 ± 0.51), while every control group held its mean — bar 644 rows -0.08 ± 0.09, line 308 rows +0.02 ± 0.15, pie 225 rows +0.11 ± 0.17, scatter 64 rows -0.08 ± 0.21, boxplot 14 rows +0.07 ± 0.38, heatmap 9 rows -0.44 ± 0.66, funnel 6 rows +0.83 ± 1.85. Seven control intervals include zero, which is the claim that matters: the instrument did not drift, so the group that moved is the change. 140 x 4.13 / 1,411 = 0.41 of the 0.39 observed. Per mark: bar 645/645 at 3.06/6.69, line 452/452 at 4.36/6.34, pie 225/227 at 2.91/6.61, scatter 64/64 at 2.72/6.53, boxplot 14/14 at 3.07/2.50, heatmap 9/9 at 0.67/2.22, funnel 6/6 at 6.00/7.50, candlestick 1/1 at 10.00/9.00. Heatmap is now the worst bucket on both axes and is the next round's target. **The think A/B arm is void, not negative.** Run 44155803661 asked for `think=off` over the same 1,418 figures and graded 244 of them before the account ran out: rows 248 onwards returned `429 余额不足或无可用资源包,请充值。` 1,174 times, in 35 minutes, and the log printed `chart_correctness 2.58` over those 244 rows as though it were a reading. That run cost one lesson and two fixes: `judgeJobsWith` stops after eight calls in a row without a reply and reports where it stopped (`aborted`), and `gradingExitCode` is red on a stopped run whatever share of the corpus it lost. No number about thinking is registered, because none was measured.

renderNote: The pixel half, recorded in the round the renderer was built: 1,286 of the 1,470 scored rows reach a PNG (87.48%), 17 are refused because a gauge states a value against a scale this contract does not carry, and 167 are the rows the recommender declines. The floor is the pair (rendered >= 1,286, failed == 0) rather than an accuracy reading: a chart that raised in Python came from this repository own emitter. Still (rendered == 1,286, failed == 0) after the column-order fix, which changed which column each figure is drawn against without changing how many figures exist: 389 of 1,464 tables were being read in JavaScript property order, five of them against an entirely empty year column. 1,418 (v9.29): four tables that had no shape reach a PNG through the melt, and 111 are re-marked without changing the count of figures -- so the floor moves by the four that are new, not by the 111 that changed.

census.note: The sweep's floor, and the first one this repository has had for a derived reading. The shipped table reads 664 of 1,470, which is the number `top1` records above from a different instrument: the classifier and the sweep agree row for row, and the identity `assertCensusReport` holds is what makes the other thirty-three rows comparable to it. Four candidates are recorded rather than all thirty-four, because four are what a decision is read off: `distribution-wide` is the table the documentation backs, and `no-share` / `no-ranking` are the two the halves guard marks as fitted — the two a reader would otherwise quote as the top of the board. `no-histogram` prices the histogram cue's whole contribution, 50 rows, which is the number the next widening has to beat. **Why this floor exists at all**: both totals in a first draft of the round that introduced the halves were six rows off, because every row in the table is priced against the shipped table and the shipped table had moved when a widening was reverted; the draft kept the numbers from the tree before the revert, and nothing refused them. A derived reading with no floor is a table that can be quoted after the tree under it changed — the same defect as a gate that prints green without measuring.

llm.instrument: eval/text2vis/llm.ts, PROMPT_VERSION 1, deepseek-chat, temperature 0, max_tokens 96, thinking absent
llm.requestNote: The request, as the arm itself records it in every artifact: prompt version 1 with a 96-token reply budget. `instrument` above is the same fact written for a reader; this is the same fact written for a comparison, because a reader cannot be asked what a file means. A local artifact from the first dispatch — version 1, a 32-token cap, 857 top-1 — sat on disk and the gate called it "inside the band, not a regression": every count in it added up, and the only thing wrong with it was the request it answered. That is the class of file this field refuses.
llm.resamples: Three dispatches of one arm with no code change moved mark 857 / 859 / 856 and label 886 / 886 / 889 — a spread of 3 rows at temperature 0. A floor without a band therefore rejects a re-sample: run 44439035718 failed at 856 against a floor of 857, which is 0.07pp and inside the instrument's own noise. 5 rows is wider than the largest observed spread and still 0.34pp, below any decision this benchmark can make. On the 96-token request that actually ships the same arm read 859, 861, 861 and 861 across four dispatches — a spread of 2 rows, because the last three restored one store instead of re-asking — so the five-row tolerance is wider than the instrument needs and is kept anyway: the wider number was measured on a prompt the repository no longer sends, and narrowing a band in the same commit that re-registers the floor would hide which of the two moved.
llm.note: The first full reading of the chart half by a model, and the floor the next dispatch is held to. 1,470 rows asked at both scales; the 515 corpus rows whose label no family names are not sent, which is a correction this reading itself produced — the run before it asked all 1,985 and scored 1,470, so 1,030 calls of 3,970 bought nothing. Zero replies were cut at the cap; the run before it had 5 cut at max_tokens 32, and the three whose cut landed just after the name were counted as answers, which is why that run read 860 top-1 and this one reads 857. `mark` offers the eleven marks this product can draw and is scored by profile.ts's own scorer, so 857 - 606 is a difference between two answers on one population. `label` offers the corpus's vocabulary and counts exact family matches: 886, of which 59 name a family no mark leads with (area, histogram, violin), which is the only scale on which those families can be hit. Cost: ¥0.604 + ¥0.649 = ¥1.25 for 2,940 calls, ¥0.0004 per row per scale. The `mark` arm's floor has since been re-registered at 861: the 857 it carried was taken on a 32-token reply budget, and the 96-token request that ships reads 859 and 861. **v9.48: 861 and 886 reproduced for Y0, and the second model priced at 875.** Run `44684484285` asked the same 1,470 rows with `deepseek-chat` and `deepseek-reasoner` in one dispatch. The chat halves were restored from the content-addressed store (2,940 of 2,940 hits, 0 calls, Y0) and read exactly the numbers above, which is the store's own receipt: the key is the request, and four commits of code changed nothing about the request. The reasoning half is the new arm — 1,469 answered, 1 unparsed, 0 truncated, **875 top-1 (59.52%)** against 861, so it clears the floor the previous round registered for it (>=861) by 14 rows. The head-to-head is in `llm.comparison`: 788 rows both arms get, 73 only the chat arm, 87 only the reasoning arm, McNemar p = 0.30. A registered arm now records its own `request`: the floor's 96-token budget is a fact about a chat endpoint, and a reasoning endpoint is sent no cap at all, so one global request could only ever exempt the second arm or refuse it. Cost is the one number this reading cannot publish — the first dispatch (run `44681062395`) bought 1,469 answers and died on a 60-second deadline before printing a bill, and the store keeps answers, not meters. **v9.49: the two arms are worth the same, and a rule that reads them together is worth 21 rows.** The routing table is now `llm.duel`: cue-led 891 decided / 828 shipped, against 863 / 807 for the chat arm alone and 875 / 818 for the reasoning one. It is registered as a priced option rather than adopted, because the six-rule correction puts the shipped gain at p = 0.28 and the router costs two calls per row.

deepseek-chat|mark.note: **v9.52: 861 -> 889.** Not a re-sample and not a better prompt: `markAnswer` now reads the question it is scoring, because one family claim depends on it. A model that answered `bar` to a question that named a histogram produced a histogram — `toChartIR` pools and bins the cells whatever arm named the bar — and the scorer was reading that chart as a bar, which is a reading of a chart nobody received. 28 rows, and the same 28 the product gained on its own path, because these are the rows where the arm and the table agree on `bar`. The 11-mark roster has no `histogram` in it, so `bar` is the only answer a model can give to a histogram question; scoring it as wrong was a defect of the instrument, and it is the reason this floor moved by +28 with no call bought.

deepseek-reasoner|mark.note: **v9.52: 875 -> 892.** The same repair as `deepseek-chat|mark`, measured on the arm that deliberates: +17 against the chat arm's +28. The two rows of difference are the finding, not the noise — the thinking arm talks itself out of `bar` on some of these questions (it answers `boxplot` or `line`, which are refused or drawn as something else), so a capability that rewards the plain answer rewards the cheaper arm more. The strong-against-weak gap on the mark scale therefore *narrows* from 14 rows to 3 while the label scale keeps its 61: deliberation buys vocabulary, and this family is answered with a word the vocabulary already had.

deepseek-reasoner|label.note: Established by run 44732340778, and the only arm of the four that had no floor: the earlier attempt answered one row, so the reading existed without a number worth recording. On the same 1,470 rows and the same 12-option list, the thinking arm reads **947 exact (64.42%)** against the chat arm's 886 (60.27%) — +61 rows, +4.15pp, and the first strong-against-weak comparison on the scale a Text2Vis paper reports. 68 of its 947 hits are families no mark leads with, so the number is a property of the *label* task rather than of this product's reach. Cost: 1,470 calls, 366,526 prompt and 365,323 completion tokens, ¥3.58, no cache hits — the label scale for this arm had never been bought.

arbitration.note: Two full dispatches priced the same six policies on the same 1,470 rows: best 861 and 863, model alone 859 and 861, product 606 both times, ceiling 994 both times. The hybrid therefore wins by 2 rows in both — the sign is stable and the size is 0.14pp — which is why the floor records the best policy's reading rather than a margin over the model. The tolerance is the model floor's, for the model floor's reason: every cell here is a function of the two answer columns, and those move by a couple of rows per re-sample. **v9.46: product 606 -> 610, ceiling 994 -> 974.** The product's answers moved onto the model's, and the union is where that shows: the derived boxplot wins 26 rows the model also gets right, and gives back 22 rows the corpus drew as a bar - twenty of which leave the union, because neither answer is right on them any more. `best` and `bestPolicy` are unchanged: model-holds still reads 863, so the routing table's maximum did not move with the product under it. Both numbers are re-registered rather than accepted as drift, because `product` is compared for equality on purpose: a deterministic rule path that changes its answer is a change to the product, not a re-sample. **v9.50: product 610 -> 614, ceiling 974 -> 970.** The five parser repairs and the whole-column `limit` changed the product's answer on 13 rows, and the arbitration prices both halves of that change. Eight of those rows move from disputed to agreed with the product now right — every one of them a row the model already had — and four move the other way, from product-right to agreed-on-a-wrong-answer. The product's own reading rises by 4 because 8 gains against 4 losses is +4. The union is the set of rows either system gets right, so the 8 enter nothing (they were already in it) and the 4 leave it: 974 -> 970. That direction is the point of registering the ceiling next to the product rather than instead of it — a product that improves by agreeing with the model makes the selector's job *smaller*, because the rows it gives up are rows only it could have won. `cue-led` 750 -> 756, `cue-any` 702 -> 704, `product-holds` 630 -> 629, `model-holds` 863 unchanged: the best policy and the policy the shipped path is held to did not move, so this round's four rows did not make the routing easier to price, they made the product closer to the arm it is being routed against. **v9.52: product 614 -> 664, best 863 -> 891, ceiling 970 -> 1020, and all three rose together.** The histogram reading lifts both systems on the same 50 rows, and the union rises by the full 50 because the rows it wins were rows *neither* answered before: the rule path had no histogram mark and the model had no histogram word in its roster, so these were rows where agreement could only ever be agreement on a wrong answer. `productRight` rises 109 -> 131 and `modelRight` holds at 356; the cells are 533 agreed-right + 131 product-only + 356 model-only = 1,020, and the disagreement falls 650 -> 645. Every policy moves up by between 50 and 52 rows (`cue-led` 756 -> 799, `cue-any` 704 -> 756, `product-holds` 629 -> 679) and the ordering is unmoved: `model-holds` is still the best policy, now at 891, which is also exactly what the shipped path decides — the identity `route` asserts row for row survives a 28-row change on the model side.
arbitration.why: This is the only gate whose artifact is derived rather than bought: no model is asked anything. It is checked anyway, because a policy that routes every row to one answer reads exactly like a policy that works, and because the two identities it carries (the disagreement partitions the population; the ceiling is the union of the three cells) are the only things that make the six readings add up to something.

ship.note: Two integers, established by run 44580426870 and reproducible for ¥0: that dispatch restored 2,940 of 2,940 answers from the store (1,470 hit, 0 miss on each scale), made no call, and read exactly what the two dispatches before it read. `decided` 863 is 861 model hits plus 2 hits on the 6 rows the model declined; `shipped` 754 is what a caller receives, and the 109 rows between the two are the vetoes, which is the whole reason both are registered instead of one. The arithmetic a reader can check: the vetoes took 220 model hits away (401 model-decided rows became table-decided, 220 of them hits) and returned 111 table hits on the 402 rows the table answered, so 863 - 220 + 111 = 754. The reading is the product *without* the second question: 754. With it, the same answers read 751 on run 44648039546 — the repair is measurably worse on exactly the rows it can reach, and `llm.repair` records that verdict. **v9.46: shipped 754 -> 793, decided 863 unchanged, changed 307 -> 171.** The derived boxplot stops the veto that was costing the most: `not-admitted` falls 223 -> 87 and the chart draws the model's own answer on those rows, which is right 39 times more often than the table's was. `decided` does not move because the policy did not: the model still holds every row it answered, so 863 is the same number for a different reason. The arithmetic a reader can check: 1199 model answers, 271 table answers, 793 hits, and 266 vetoes (144 wide + 87 not-admitted + 35 unchartable) accounting for the rows where the chart is not what the decision said. **v9.47: shipped 793 -> 807, decided 863 unchanged, changed 171 -> 138.** The reshape stopped being a preference. `wideIR` used to hard-code one mark and `assistedChartIR` used to return before asking the advisor on this shape, on the stated ground that one line per entity is the only reading a table written sideways produces — a claim about the first implementation, not about the reshape. The corpus prices it: of the 144 wide tables, 71 are labelled Line and 53 Bar, the model names `bar` on 33 of them and is right on 20 against 6 the line was winning. `wide` is therefore no longer a reason at all, `not-admitted` rises 87 -> 104 because a wide table whose model answer is a pie or a scatter is now refused with a sentence instead of skipped, and the rows the table answers fall 186 -> 144. The arithmetic a reader can check: 1,326 model answers + 144 table answers = 1,470; 5 no-advice + 104 not-admitted + 35 unchartable = 144; 138 rows drew an answer other than the decision's against 139 vetoes, the difference being one vetoed row whose table answer happened to be the decision's mark. The model arm cost nothing again (1,470 of 1,470 answers restored, 0 calls). **v9.50: shipped 807 unchanged, decided 863 unchanged.** Two movements underneath, in opposite directions. `unchartable` falls 35 -> 28 and `not-admitted` rises 104 -> 109, so the table answers 142 rows instead of 144 and the chart is right on the same 807. The fall is the repairs: a `nan` read as a number and a column of nothing no longer counted as a column give the table an answer to draw on rows that had none. The rise is the price of the same admissions: a profile that admits a measure can admit a mark the table cannot hold, and the model's answer on such a row is refused with a sentence where it used to be skipped. The arithmetic a reader can check: 1,328 model answers + 142 table answers = 1,470; 5 no-advice + 109 not-admitted + 28 unchartable = 142; 136 rows drew an answer other than the decision's against 137 vetoes, the difference still being the one vetoed row whose table answer happened to be the decision's mark. Net zero on `shipped` is the reading, and it is not a disappointment: a table that can read a cell it used to drop draws a chart more often, not a better one. **v9.51: shipped 807 -> 810, decided 863 unchanged.** The candlestick's axis stopped being a calendar. Three rows of the refusal bill were the whole of that family — a week written `Day 1 … Day 7`, four numbers per row, one row per period — and the table refused all three for lacking a date axis they did not need. A mark that reads a sequence has two spellings of it: a date column, or a label column with one value per row. `not-admitted` therefore falls 109 -> 106 and the rows the table answers 142 -> 139, all three of them drawn as the model named and right, which is the bill's own row reading 'a derivation could win: at most 3' paid in full. The arithmetic a reader can check: 1,331 model answers + 139 table answers = 1,470; 5 no-advice + 106 not-admitted + 28 unchartable = 139; 133 rows drew an answer other than the decision's against 134 vetoes. The rule arm cannot see this change and its readings are unchanged (top-1 614, shortlist 718, declined 28) because `profileAnswer` prices the product from profiles alone and a row count is exactly what a sequence claim needs; the shipped reading is the one that prices it, which is why the floor is registered there. **v9.52: decided 863 -> 891, shipped 810 -> 843.** The same reading, priced where a caller meets it. The arithmetic a reader can check: 1,334 model answers + 136 table answers = 1,470; 5 no-advice + 104 not-admitted + 27 unchartable = 136; 130 rows drew an answer other than the decision's. `decided` rose by 28 — the rows where the model said `bar` to a histogram question — and `shipped` by 36, and the eight rows of difference are the part worth reading: `not-admitted` fell 109 -> 104 and `unchartable` 28 -> 27 because the reading asks no admission rule at all (there is nothing to admit: the rows are the bins), so six rows that used to be answered by the table are now answered by the model's own `bar` and drawn as bins. The gap between the two counts is 48 rows, down from 56: a veto costs what the table's answer is worth against the model's, and this round made the table's answer worth more on exactly the rows the veto touches.
ship.why: The floor is registered on `shipped` because that is the number a caller experiences, and on `decided` because that is the identity against the arbitration policy: a drift in `decided` is a policy change nobody asked for, and a drift in `shipped` is the product disagreeing with its own description. They are not ordered and the first draft of `ship.ts` was wrong to assert they were: a veto replaces the model's mark with the table's, so `shipped` can read above or below `decided` and an alternating bar/pie arm made it read 433 against 420. What survives is the row-by-row constraint the artifact carries: a chart is one of the two answers, and it changes only to the table's.

repair.note: The second question, priced twice: once on the 223 rows the admissions refused (run 44648039546) and again on the 87 that are left after the derived boxplot was admitted (run 44661951720). The first reading is the one that made the admission the target rather than the prompt: 144 of the 223 refusals were `boxplot`, the model was naming the one mark that would have said what the question asked, and a shorter list cannot invent a picture. On the residual 87 the short list is a wash and slightly ahead - 16 right against the table's 15 on the same rows, 86 asked, 43 calls, Y0.0136 - which is inside the noise of a 15-row comparison and does not overturn the verdict. **v9.50: the population under this verdict is 109 rows, not 104, and the reading is not re-bought.** The parser repairs moved the refused set up by five, so the numbers above were bought on a population that no longer exists. The verdict is left alone because it has now been `rejected` on 223, 87 and 104 rows for one reason — a two-row edge on a hundred is not a signal — and a fourth purchase on 109 would buy the same sentence. What would change it is a *drawable* mark, and the refusal bill prices that instead of a prompt: of the 109, the only family a derivation wins honestly is candlestick's 3 rows, because the label says the candle's own words; scatter's 32 and boxplot's 9 are owed to a table whose columns are one measure and one category, so a derived scatter is a bar chart with round ends and a renaming is not a capability. **v9.51: the 3 rows this note named as the only honest debt are now drawn.** The candlestick admits a label column with one value per row, so the refused population is 106 and no family in the bill is left that a derivation would win honestly. The verdict stays `rejected`: the second question still has nothing to buy.
repair.why: The verdict is `rejected`, and the reason it is recorded here rather than deleted with the code is that the code still works: a shorter list is a real question and a model answers it. What the measurement says is that the answer is not better than the rule table on the rows where the model's first answer was impossible. The distribution of the 223 refusals explains it: 144 `boxplot` ("a boxplot reads five numbers per row" — the mark is drawable only when the table already carries a five-number summary), 36 `scatter` ("needs two measures"), 8 `heatmap`, and the rest one or two each. The model was not naming a mark at random; it was naming the one mark that would have said what the question asked, and no list without that mark can hold the answer. So the lever is a *drawable* mark — a boxplot computed from raw rows — not a better prompt, and this file is the receipt that the cheaper hypothesis was tried first. **v9.47: re-priced on the 104 refusals the new admissions leave, run 44673494103: 103 asked, 101 answered, 22 right against the table's 20 on the same rows, 60 calls, Y0.0181 (43 answers restored). The verdict stays `rejected` for the third time and for the same reason — two rows on a hundred is not a signal — but the population moved in a way worth recording: the 144 `boxplot` refusals that made the admission the target are gone, the `wide` rows that could not be asked are gone, and what is left is 104 rows where the model named a mark the table genuinely cannot hold.

comparison.note: Two arms, one dispatch, one corpus download: the chat arm was restored from the store for Y0 and the reasoning arm was bought once. The discordant pairs are 73 against 87, so the direction is the reasoning model and the size is not a signal: +14 rows at p = 0.30. Where it wins is where the answer is a shape the question names rather than a shape the table suggests (pie +13 of 182, line +8 of 394); where it loses is the two families this product derives rather than reads (scatter -5 of 104, boxplot -3 of 90). That is the reading worth keeping: deliberation buys vocabulary, not structure. And the number that decides it is not either reading: the union with the rule table is 970 for the chat arm and 974 for the reasoning one, so +14 rows alone is +4 rows in union: 505 of the chat arm's 861 hits and 515 of the reasoning arm's 875 are rows the product already had right, which is why 14 rows of separation between two arms is 4 rows of separation between their unions. The floor is registered at 875 anyway, because a floor records what an arm reads, not whether it is worth buying. **v9.50: the cells move with the product, and the sign of the union delta flips.** unionA 974 -> 970, unionB 973 -> 974, `product` 610 -> 614 in both. Neither arm changed; the product did. This is recorded because the sentence above was read off numbers where the product contributed the same 610 answers to both cells, and it does not survive the product moving: at 610 the chat arm's union was the larger by 1, at 614 the reasoning arm's is the larger by 4. So 'deliberation buys vocabulary, not structure' stands on the family cells (pie +13 of 182, line +8 of 394) and not on the union — a union is a property of the pair, and a claim about which arm buys more of it is a claim about the product as much as about the arms. **v9.52: both 788 -> 800, aOnly 73 -> 89, bOnly 87 -> 92, neither 522 -> 489, p 0.3041 -> 0.8819.** The histogram reading is not a property of either arm — it is a property of the product both arms are scored against — so the *pairing* moves with it, and it moves differently for each arm because the arms answer histogram questions differently: the chat arm says `bar` on 28 of them, the reasoning arm on 17. Both gain, neither gains differentially (p = 0.88), and the union moves 970/974 -> 1020/1023. The sentence this table exists to test is unchanged and is now better supported: deliberation buys vocabulary (the label scale, +61 rows) and not structure (the mark scale, +3).

duel.note: The six rules `arbitrate.ts` already prices, repriced between two arms on the same 1,470 rows, at Y0: the answers of run `44684484285` are on disk and this is a re-analysis of them. The two arms agree on 1,234 rows (788 of them right) and disagree on 236, of which the chat arm wins 73 and the reasoning one 87. `cue-led` reads **891**, which is +16 over the better single arm and +30 over the chat arm; the pairing against the chat arm is 74 gained / 44 lost (p = 0.0073), against the reasoning arm 29 / 13 (p = 0.0195, and 0.117 with a six-rule Bonferroni), and on the *shipped* charts 61 gained / 39 lost (p = 0.0352, 0.211 corrected). So the direction is the rule and the size is not an established effect: the vetoes redistribute far more rows than the rule changes. What the shipped column says is nonetheless the number a caller would receive -- 807 (chat), 819 (reasoner), **829** (routed) -- and 829 is 56.39% of the population against 54.90%. A one-call alternative was priced and is worse: the product against the reasoning arm, through the same rules, reads 766 (`cue-led`) against the reasoning arm's own 875, because the cue rules only pay when the two answers are of comparable quality. Run `44696562624` reproduced it in a clean environment on a commit that added the command: cue-led 891, shipped 828 / 818 / 807 (829 / 819 / 807 after the parser repairs of round 179), reasoner 875, chat 861 — and the two arms were replayed from the store for Y0 with all 2,940 answers reported as `unmetered`, which is the meter fix saying exactly what it knows: those entries were written before the store kept tokens, so the reading's own cost is unknown rather than free. **v9.51: the shipped column moves 3, 2 and 2 rows, and one pairing crosses its threshold.** The candlestick's axis stopped being a calendar and three rows stopped being refused, which is three charts for the chat arm and two for each router that spends a call only where it must: 810 / 821 / 831 against 807 / 819 / 829. `cue-led` holds at 891 on the decisions, so the *rule* is unmoved and what moved is what a caller receives under it. The pairing against the chat arm reads 61 gained and 40 lost at p = 0.0460 (was 61 / 39, p = 0.0352) — still under 0.05 and still over it after a six-rule Bonferroni, so the direction holds and the size was never the claim. The three rows are the whole of the movement, and they are the same three the refusal bill priced at 'at most 3'. **v9.52: every policy rises, and the router's lead widens 9 -> 25 rows.** Two repairs, both of them the same fact seen from two sides. First, the histogram reading is a capability of the *product*, so a `bar` answer to a histogram question now ships bins whoever named the bar: chat 861 -> 889 and reasoner 875 -> 892. Second, `duelOf` was wrapping the left arm's mark in a one-element family list, so the router was pricing one arm on a reading the other arm got through `markAnswer` — a bar answer to a histogram question scored as a bar for `chat` and as a histogram for `profileAnswer`. It now asks `markAnswer` like every other reader, which is why the disagreement falls 248 -> 236: the two arms agree on 12 more rows because 12 of them were never in dispute, only mis-scored. `cue-led` 891 -> 917 is the best rule by 25 rows over the better single arm (was 9), and the paired read against the chat arm is 65 gained / 43 lost at p = 0.0428 — unchanged in direction, and now with a margin that does not depend on one arm's histogram answers. Ceiling 965 -> 981: the union of the two arms, up by the rows each one gained.

prior.note: Five priors and the two-call router, priced in the same unit on the same 1,470 rows, at Y0: the answers of run `44696562624` are on disk and this is a re-analysis of them. A prior decides which arm to call from what is free before the call -- the cue table's first mark, whether it fired at all, and the recommender's own mark -- so unlike `llm.duel` it prices a router a caller can actually deploy at one call per row. `cue-gate` is the one that reads best: spend the thinking call only on the 305 questions no cue reads, which ships **815** for 1,165 plain calls and 305 thinking ones -- 8 of the 21 charts the two-call router buys, for 27% of its bill. `table-agrees` ships 816 at 4.27x the plain price, `reasoner` ships 818 at 7.72x, and `table-refused` buys its 35 thinking calls and ships **nothing**: the recommender's refusal is not a signal that deliberation helps, and that prior is dominated. The number that decides is the marginal one -- yuan per *additional* chart over the default: cue-gate **Y0.109**, table-agrees Y0.228, the two-call router **Y0.230**, reasoner Y0.383 -- so the router that reads both answers buys its 21 charts at more than twice the unit price of the one-call prior's 8, and that ordering is r-free: cue-gate's marginal is 305(r-1) yuan / 8 against the router's 1470r yuan / 21, which is lower for every r >= 0. The ratio r itself is a parameter rather than a measurement, because the 2,940 answers on disk were written before the store kept meters; the default 7.72 is the one live reasoning call this project metered (Y0.00329 against a plain call's measured Y0.000426, the receipt being Y1.2521 for 2,940 calls). Every conclusion is stated as the ratio at which it would stop holding: cue-gate is the cheaper chart than the default only below x1.048, table-agrees below x1.023, reasoner below x1.014, and the two-call router below **x0.026** -- so at any price a provider has ever charged, buying both answers is the most expensive way to obtain a chart this corpus can measure. A thinking call is one prompt of the same length with a longer completion, so r is bounded below by 1: no reading here is sensitive to a ratio smaller than the one that would make deliberation free. **Re-read in round 179, at Y0, after two parser repairs** — `nan` read as a printed absence rather than as text, and a column every cell of which is an absence dropped from the profile — which moved the product’s own reading from 610 to 614 top-1 and 713 to 718 shortlist and these five routers by +1, +1, -2, 0 and +1: reasoner 819, cue-gate 816, table-agrees **814**, table-refused 807, both 829. One line went down, and it is stated rather than smoothed: `table-agrees` spends its thinking call where the cue lead and the recommender disagree, so a recommender that answers differently on nine rows asks for deliberation in two places it used to keep to itself. The ordering the table exists for is unmoved: `cue-gate` still buys its charts at under half the two-call router’s unit price, at every ratio. **Re-read in round 180 on run `44732340778`, at Y0, after the candlestick stopped needing a calendar**: chat 807 -> 810, reasoner 819 -> 821, cue-gate 816 -> 818, table-agrees 814 -> 816, table-refused 807 -> 810, both 829 -> 831. Every router gains, and the reason is the same three rows in each: the candlestick now answers a table whose periods are spelled `Day 1 … Day 7`, which is three charts for the default arm and two for each of the routers — the third row is one a router was already getting right by another route, so a router that adds a rule in front of a better arm gains less than the arm itself. The ordering is unmoved and one marginal moved a lot: `table-agrees` now buys 6 charts instead of 7 with the same thinking calls, so its price per *additional* chart rises Y0.228 -> Y0.342 while `cue-gate` holds at Y0.109 with 8. The claim the table exists for survives untouched — the one-call prior is still the cheaper chart by a factor of three, at every ratio. **Re-read in round 181 on the same answers (run `44732340778`, Y0), after the histogram reading**: chat 810 -> 843, reasoner 821 -> 849, cue-gate 818 -> 851, table-agrees 816 -> 847, table-refused 810 -> 843, both 831 -> 865. Every router gains, and the ordering is unmoved: `cue-gate` is still the one-call router that buys the most, at 8 charts over the default for Y0.109 each, and `table-agrees` still costs Y0.507 for each of its 4. One price moved in the direction that matters for the argument this table makes: the default path's cost per chart fell Y0.000773 -> Y0.000743 because the same Y1.09 buys 843 charts instead of 810 — a capability that costs nothing to run is a capability that lowers the price of every chart behind it. The two-call router `both` gains 22 charts (843 -> 865) for 8.72x the price per row, so the claim the table exists for survives untouched: the one-call prior is still the cheaper chart by an order of magnitude.
